newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba confidence in German EMU readiness waning.
newsitem.headline: Buba confidence in German EMU readiness waning.

text.p: The Bundesbank's confidence that Germany will qualify for European monetary union is showing signs of waning, raising expectations that rules for membership may have to be relaxed to accommodate Europe's most important economy.

Publicly expressing doubts not often heard from leading policy-makers, members of the Bundesbank's council have in the last week raised the possibility Germany will not cut its budget deficit to the level mandated by the Maastricht Treaty.
Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher took one of the strongest stands on monetary union, saying flatly "Germany will not achieve the deficit criterion in 1997."

Although not aimed at delivering a setback to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), remarks such as Kuehbacher's reveal the awkward position of the central bank, insisting on the one hand on tough EMU membership criteria, but finding a place for a less-than fully qualified Germany on the other.

"Everyone at the Bundesbank is starting to worry about whether Germany can qualify for monetary union and some there do not think they can," said Adolf Rosenstock, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt.

Although the Maastricht Treaty lays down rules for a range of economic indicators, the most difficult for Germany and other European nations has been to trim budget deficits to a stated goal of three percent of gross domestic product.
"I do not yet see quite clearly if Germany will be able to fulfill the three percent goal," Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said this week.
Only 18 months ago, Germany ranked clearly as Europe's leader on issues of fiscal discipline, proclaiming loudly that its long-term aim was to cut its budget deficit to one percent of GDP.

Yet that ratio stood at 3.8 percent in 1996 for Germany and most private economists see it falling to slightly above the three percent level by the end of the year -- despite promises from the finance ministry that the deficit will be 2.9 pct.

Bundesbank council member Helmut Hesse, agreed that Germany might not qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), telling a German newspaper that at least in theory, monetary union may initially only consist of a group of small nations that meet the Maastricht targets.
The decision on which nations will make up EMU will be made in spring 1998, based on their 1997 economic performances.
But although doubt about Germany's ability to strictly meet EMU targets appears to be growing, Bundesbank council members have stopped short of calling for EMU to be abandoned or delayed.

In remarks that seem to run counter to virtually universal calls for Maastricht rules to be strictly applied, some of those doubting Germany's EMU position have called on European nations to find a way to include Germany nonetheless.
Welteke said, for example, "Neither the three percent (deficit) nor the 60 percent (national debt-to GDP) criteria are criteria that must lead a country to not joining EMU if it breaches them."
Kuehbacher added, "Germany should be there from the beginning."
The treaty leaves room for such a weakening of the targets if progress is being made in cutting deficits and a clause allowing them to plead special circumstances were to be used.
For many here, delaying EMU would be worse than going ahead with the project even if Maastricht targets have to be fudged.
Delaying EMU now, they argue, would unleash a rush of capital into Germany, swelling the value of the mark and playing havoc with Germany's ability to export its way out of prolonged economic slump.
"I see a budget deficit of 3.1 percent for 1997. With figures that close to the EMU criteria, EMU will go forward," said Christian Sobotta, economist LGT Asset Management in Frankfurt.
